statement: A triangle has sides of length 7, 10 and x, where x is a whole number. For how many values of x is the triangle obtuse?

choices.misconception: I only checked the case where x is the longest side, missing the triangles whose obtuse angle is opposite the side of length 10.
I counted the acute triangles, the 13 possible triangles minus the 8 obtuse ones.
I forgot the triangle inequality, so I also counted x = 1, 2 and 3 as obtuse triangles.
I counted every whole number x that makes a triangle, from 4 to 16, without testing for an obtuse angle.

hints: An obtuse angle sits opposite the longest side.
First list the values of x that make a triangle at all. Then split into cases by which side is longest, and compare the square of the longest side with the sum of the squares of the other two.
x runs from 4 to 16. If x is the longest side you need x² > 49 + 100. If 10 is the longest side you need 49 + x² < 100.

solutions.reliable: The triangle inequality needs 10 - 7 < x < 10 + 7, so x is 4 to 16, which is 13 values. Case 1, x is the longest side: obtuse when x² > 7² + 10² = 149, so x = 13, 14, 15, 16, which is 4 values. Case 2, 10 is the longest side: obtuse when 7² + x² < 10², so x² < 51, giving x = 4, 5, 6, 7, which is 4 values. The side 7 can never be longest. That makes 4 + 4 = 8. No value gives a right angle, since 51 and 149 are not square numbers. The transferable idea: split by which side is longest, and never forget the triangle inequality.
solutions.elegant: Count the acute ones instead. The triangle is right-angled at x = √51 and at x = √149, so it is acute exactly when x is strictly between them, which is x = 8 to 12, five values. The other 13 - 5 = 8 triangles are obtuse.

whyOnTest: Counting obtuse triangles combines the triangle inequality with the longest-side test, and each forgotten case is one of the choices.
